# Testing moringa if it has been planted correctly

How do I test if a Moringa Olifera tree has been planted correctly using Moringa seed or seeds?

Comment: It grows into a tree (somewhat like a mimosa... IMO), a bit of how you planted it isn't going to matter much I don't think.... the usual things apply (pests/diseases, regarding watering, don't plant too deep, if you're attempting to garden assuming fertility and available soil nutrients, then don't assume they are there... etc...)

## Answer (5)

Germination time is usually between 5-12 days, so in observing this, simply provide the ideal growth conditions. Keep in mind that Moringa does not transplant well, so it's best to start where it's introduced. Here is a guide to some ideal conditions:

> **Seeds**
>
> Plant seeds 1in. (2cm) deep.
> The minimum pot size is 18in. (45cm) deep and 8in. (20cm) wide.
> The soil should be well drained, and rich. One part sand, one part loam and one part composted manure. Retains water, however, drains well in order that the roots get plenty of oxygen. pH of 6.3 to 7.0 (slightly acidic to neutral).
> Seedlings require plenty of sunlight. Soil must be kept moist.
> It's best to use seeds within 1 year of harvest.
>
> **Germination**
>
> The optimum temperature is 25 C (70° F), although any temperature lower than 15 C (60° F) or greater than 35 C (90° F) essentially prevents germination.
> The seeds will germinate in less than 2 weeks, however, it can take up to a month and as little as 5 days for the sprout to emerge.
>
> **Optimum Growing Conditions**
>
> Sun... they need to be in the hottest, sunniest spot in your yard.
> Moisture... rain or water should not fall directly on the leaves reducing the potential for disease formation.
> Soil... pH 6.3 to 7.0; this is the ideal acidity level for Moringa to grow in.
>
> **Note:**
>
> Avoid over-watering your Moringa Tree! I repeat. Do not over water!

Remember each plant has it's data sheet, so it's good to have an understanding of that plants biology before you jump into planting it. Take a look at Moringa's General Data Sheet, as that will not only give you a good idea of the plants biology but also inform you of some of the United States Humidity averages and inform you of the hardiness zones for this tree.

Additionally, if you would like a more visual and in depth guide. Take a look at this Moringa horticulture publication and this shorter Moringa spacing article. Both will give you the bottom line and a very great understanding of this plant and how to maintain it in some early stages. If I can recommend an approach to plant testing, I would say visualize a successful harvest. If the plant meets all the recommended prerequisites, you are off to a good start.

Lastly, a final bonus tip. The plant grows quicker and is ready for consumption as soon as 6 weeks! However, if you want seeds be prepared to wait up to a year. Impatience will not help you cultivate your plants, only time and the observation of it.

## Answer (2)

The shallow, fibrous root system means transplanting Moringa is relatively easy. When grown from seed, the first requirements are:

1) Cull seed that show obvious signs of disease or damage.

2) Plant the seeds 1" deep in their permanent location. Mulching can help retain water in the upper layers of soil.

If you have mistakenly applied too much compost or manure, the trees roots will atrophy. If no other trees are showing signs of nutrient deficiencies, it is likely not a fertilizer or nutrition issue.

3) Monitor daily for sprouting and initial signs of disease. If you are planting many moringa in rows, put the date next to each plant so you know how old each tree is. Root damage (accidents happen) will delay vertical growth and sometimes branch growth noticeably.

4) If you are planting seeds in place, don't forget that it is easier to water and manage small areas effectively. Plant seeds in small squares then move on to the next. Pay attention to vines and other competing growth. Morning glory, butterfly pea, cowpea, black eye pea, and various other pigeon peas grow quickly and can crowd a moringa unless controlled.

5) Water daily, all around the plant, but nothing in contact with stem/trunk. It doesn't need much because it will rot, but you want to establish early of the location of water to encourage shallow and fibrous root development. (overwatering vs old/dried out seeds are the most common mistakes that cause plant failure with Moringa). Don't worry so much about always watering the same area, you want to establish that water is distributed shallow and throughout the top inch of soil.

6) Follow growth. Moringa show initial sprouting with the initial leaves being one single oval followed by two ovals. After 4-5 leaves, they will begin "taking off". If you grow in rows, you might want to create a stake or write the planting date on a piece of paper next to each moringa to understand which ones need more attention.
